channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Nearly half of Australian health courses fail to mention sex and gender differences
item.description: Nearly half of Australia's accredited health and medical degrees do not mention sex or gender in a single course unit, according to a national review by the Center for Sex and Gender Equity in Health and Medicine at The George Institute for Global Health, despite extensive evidence that many conditions present differently in women, men and gender-diverse people.

item.title: Medicare boost needed for Australia's 1.6 million cancer survivors
item.description: More than 1.6 million Australians living with and beyond cancer could benefit from proposed Medicare reforms to increase subsidized allied health visits, a move backed by new Flinders University–led research.

item.title: Fingertip study reveals pain threshold during millimeter-wave exposure
item.description: Wireless technologies using millimeter waves are becoming increasingly important for high-speed communication, but their effects on human health need to be better understood. Heating of the skin is a well-established effect of exposure at these frequencies, yet the temperature at which people begin to experience pain remains uncertain. Previous studies using different heat sources have reported varying pain thresholds, while evidence from direct millimeter-wave exposure in highly sensitive areas, such as the fingertip, has been limited. Understanding when sensations progress from warmth to pain could help inform safer exposure guidelines.

item.title: Psilocybin may improve a difficult-to-treat symptom of depression, study finds
item.description: New research from the University of Colorado Anschutz suggests that psilocybin may help improve anhedonia, the loss of interest or ability to experience pleasure, in people with treatment-resistant depression. In a clinical trial, researchers found significant improvement in this difficult-to-treat symptom eight weeks after treatment, offering new insight into psilocybin's potential role in depression care.

item.title: Understanding epilepsy and seizures: Q&A with epileptologist
item.description: Epilepsy, a chronic neurological condition of the central nervous system, affects millions of people, with overactive or misfiring electrical signals in the brain leading to recurrent, unprovoked seizures.

item.title: FDA approves first factor XIa inhibitor for secondary stroke prevention
item.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Sunharbo (asundexian) 50 mg tablets, in combination with antiplatelet therapy, to reduce the risk for stroke in adults following a recent mild-to-moderate noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk transient ischemic attack (TIA).

item.title: New review protocol outlines plan to evaluate quit-smoking support for ADHD and autism
item.description: Published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, the protocol "Smoking cessation interventions in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or autism spectrum disorder (ASD)" was developed by the South East Smokefree Alliance in collaboration with academics at the University of Bristol.

item.title: Nearly 1 in 10 US adults report having chronic hand eczema
item.description: Chronic hand eczema (CHE) is common, impacting nearly 1 in 10 U.S. adults, according to a study published online Nov. 11 in JAMA Dermatology.

item.title: FDA approves new drug for advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
item.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Janssen Biotech's Rybrevant Faspro (amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj) for the treatment of adults with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) whose disease has progressed during or after receipt of platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

item.title: Paintball-related eye injuries declined 84.5% from 2005 to 2025
item.description: Paintball-related ocular injuries seen at U.S. emergency departments declined by 84.5% from 2005 to 2025, according to a research letter published online Nov. 5 in JAMA Ophthalmology.

item.title: Defibrillator drones could arrive ahead of ambulances in hundreds of cardiac arrest cases
item.description: Drones carrying defibrillators could arrive ahead of ambulances at hundreds of cardiac arrest incidents each year, potentially creating opportunities for earlier treatment, according to new research. The study, published in the journal Reliability Engineering & System Safety, also found they could improve emergency response coverage in parts of Scotland.

item.title: Family doctor shortage spurs new models of care
item.description: Dr. Aaron Block graduated from medical school carrying a quarter-million dollars of medical debt and got hired as a family medicine doctor for a health network.

item.title: Beer, but not wine, linked to higher risk of kidney injury
item.description: Regular drinkers of beer or spirits may face a significantly greater risk of acute kidney injury, according to a new study that analyzed data from more than 250,000 U.K. adults. However, the same association was not found for wine drinkers.

item.title: Vest that maps heart's electrical activity could flag health risks
item.description: A vest that reads the heart's electrical signals could detect older people with risky age-related changes in their hearts, according to a study presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions conference held in Chicago Nov. 6–9.

item.title: Large and very small waist sizes linked to heightened death risk across weight range
item.description: Both large and very small waist sizes are linked to a heightened risk of death across a broad range of body weights, finds a large study of more than 17 million adults, published online in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health.

item.title: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs linked to inadequate intake of key nutrients in some people
item.description: Drugs taken to suppress appetite, such as Wegovy and Mounjaro, are associated with inadequate intakes of key nutrients and energy in some people, finds a small exploratory study published in the journal BMJ Nutrition Prevention & Health.

item.title: Many claims for health tests marketed to UK consumers are unsubstantiated
item.description: Many of the claims made for the benefits of health tests marketed to U.K. consumers are unsubstantiated, with little information provided on their potential harms and limitations, finds an assessment of the websites of 50 commercial test vendors, published in the journal BMJ Open.

item.title: First evidence from a Chinese population supports review of long-term blood monitoring for local clozapine use
item.description: An international research team led by the Department of Psychiatry, School of Clinical Medicine, LKS Faculty of Medicine of the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed), has completed a long-term population-based research study to improve care for people with treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS), the most severe form of this mental health condition. The findings reinforce the importance of timely access to clozapine and provide the first large-scale evidence from a Chinese population to support a review of Hong Kong's long-term blood monitoring requirements.

item.title: Implanted electrodes restore function after severe muscle loss in early tests
item.description: Traumatic muscle injuries, whether from battlefield wounds, gunshots, surgical resections, or major open fractures, can cause volumetric muscle loss (VML), the loss of so much tissue that the muscle cannot regenerate on its own. Recovery typically brings chronic inflammation, scarring, and permanent weakness. Current treatments remain palliative, with none reliably restoring the lost muscle.

item.title: Chronic loneliness increases dementia risk by 38%, but occasional loneliness appears harmless, 30-year study finds
item.description: A new study that tracked people over the course of 30 years finds that only chronic, persistent loneliness is strongly linked with dementia.

item.title: Alzheimer's disease protein atlas reveals hidden cell-type biology
item.description: Alzheimer's disease can affect almost the entire brain, but how different cell types are specifically affected is not fully understood. To address this gap, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital scientists developed a cell type–specific protein atlas using brains from mouse models of Alzheimer's disease. By combining and comparing multiple types of data, they identified more than 3,000 proteins with altered levels across a range of cell types, 78% of which had not been captured before.

item.title: Alcohol, drug abuse, suicide: Is Europe really safe from America's 'deaths of despair' epidemic?
item.description: In the United States, life expectancy diverged from Europe before it stopped rising during the 2010s, even before the COVID-19 pandemic. The economists Anne Case and Angus Deaton gave a name to a phenomenon that was then booming, partly explaining this trend: "deaths of despair," which have soared since the turn of the 21st century, especially among middle-aged white people without a college degree.

item.title: Forgetful neural networks could shed light on how humans learn
item.description: How the brain learns is one of the biggest unsolved mysteries in science. Researchers in artificial intelligence from the University of Groningen (the Netherlands) and KU Leuven (Belgium) hope that a specific type of forgetting in artificial neural networks will help to capture what is happening in the human brain. The study is published in the journal Trends in Cognitive Sciences.

item.title: As measles cases mount, new report highlights safety of early vaccination for infants
item.description: As Americans prepare for holiday travel amid a nationwide measles resurgence and diminished federal public health communications, a new report from the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy's (CIDRAP's) Vaccine Integrity Project (VIP) at the University of Minnesota highlights data showing that infants as young as 6 months can safely receive the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.

item.title: For military veterans with PTSD and alcohol use disorder, MDMA-assisted therapy may be safe, effective
item.description: The first study of a program that uses the drug MDMA to treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) plus alcohol use disorder in military veterans has concluded with promising results.

item.title: Regenerated bone keeps maturing after its shape is largely restored, study reveals
item.description: Regeneration is often judged by what researchers can see—whether missing tissue has returned and its shape has been restored. But a new Texas A&M study shows that bone may continue to mature mechanically beneath the surface even after it appears whole.

item.title: Your gut bacteria help your body keep track of time, and when you eat influences how much nutrition you get from food
item.description: How your body processes food is significantly influenced by daily rhythms tied to 24-hour light-dark cycles. In new research published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe, my colleagues and I found that the microbes living in your gut are the hidden timekeepers behind this system.

item.title: Alzheimer's blood marker may help estimate cognitive impairment risk up to 10 years ahead
item.description: A blood biomarker for Alzheimer's disease may help estimate a cognitively healthy person's risk of developing mild cognitive impairment or dementia over the next five or 10 years, according to a new Mayo Clinic study in JAMA Neurology.

item.title: Brain clock gene influences alcohol consumption differently in female and male mice, study shows
item.description: A gene that helps regulate the body's internal clock may influence alcohol consumption differently in males and females, according to new Concordia research.

item.title: Novel algorithm predicts brain surgery outcomes in dystonia patients
item.description: Less than 5% of patients with dystonia—a debilitating neurological movement disorder—undergo deep brain stimulation (DBS) treatment, even though it is one of the few interventions that directly target the abnormal brain processes underlying the condition. The surgical treatment is highly underutilized, likely due to its invasiveness and the lack of objective markers of who may benefit. Even among those who undergo surgery, outcomes vary widely, depending on patient characteristics and external influences.
